question: A large rectangle is partitioned into four rectangles by two segments parallel to its sides. The areas of three of the resulting rectangles are shown. What is the area of the fourth rectangle? \[\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline 6 & 14\\ \hline \text{?} & 35\\ \hline\end{array}\]
solution:
The two rectangles in the right column have the same width. Since rectangle area equals width times height, their area ratio equals their height ratio. Thus the bottom row is
\[
\frac{35}{14}=\frac52
\]
times as tall as the top row.

The same two row heights occur in the left column, whose two rectangles also share a width. Its bottom area is therefore \(5/2\) times its top area:
\[
6\cdot\frac52=\boxed{15}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\text{B}\).

edges.reason: The target explicitly distinguishes boundary length from area. Perimeter meaning is required for that contrast, not all rectangle/square perimeter computations.
Two-digit columns support larger numerical areas. Repeated unit-square counts or decomposed multiplication can also compute an area, so no fixed dimension range is imposed by this preparation link.
edges.scope: computing areas with two-digit side lengths

edges.reason: The tiled-region interpretation explains what length times width counts. The Geometric Measurement Progression develops that interpretation before treating multiplication as a formula; knowing the formula alone does not certify the tiling procedure.
edges.scope: Understanding rectangle and square area formulas as counts of square units

edges.reason: The rectangle/square area formulas count equal square units, so the meaning of area and its uniform unit are part of the asserted result.
edges.scope: interpreting length times width as unit-square count

edges.reason: Fraction division prepares ratio values with fractional terms. The target expressly permits a simple ratio, and a whole-number pair such as 6 to 3 needs only ordinary division; no fraction-by-fraction division is universal.
Contexts such as price, quantity and total, or speed, time and distance, supply familiar examples. Direct proportion can be learned through other contexts like side length and perimeter.
Direct proportion rests on a constant ratio value, which is ratio meaning. Proportion equations matter only when problems are solved by setting up a proportion.

The criteria identify an invariant ratio and use its value to find the other quantity. This requires the quotient meaning of a ratio, without the additional cross-product property of proportions. Root checked both endpoint-based reviews; each identifies the stated content or conditional method rather than a curriculum-order claim.
edges.scope: Interpreting the constant ratio and using its value in direct proportion
